reader.title: Pursuit of Mr. Verdun by a Kentucky lynch mob
bases: A mob seeking to hang a supposed murderer chased Verdun and fired bullets into his carriage, but no one was reported hurt or killed and the papers state no racial element (A1, A3).

No one was killed: the pursuers, called a 'mob' and 'lynchers' who wished to hang a murderer, overtook Verdun and let him go once the mistake was found (A1, A3); the size of the group is not given beyond 'a mob' and 'eine Schaar Berittener' (A3).

Every English copy is the same unattributed paragraph (A1, A2, A4-A7), and the German version (A3) tells the same story with added details that may come from a fuller original; no local Kentucky report was found.

summary.text: The pursuit of Mr. Verdun by a Kentucky lynch mob was an incident, reported in August 1881, in which a mob that wished to hang a murderer mistook a man named Verdun for him and chased him along a road, firing into his carriage.
No one was reported hurt, and once Verdun was overtaken the mistake was settled over drinks.
The first known report ran it as a comic item under the head "Kentucky Manners of the Road," and the paragraph was reprinted widely.
The reports name no town, county or date, saying only that the incident took place in Kentucky.
A German-language version printed in Washington on 20 August described Verdun as a traveling salesman ("Geschäftsreisender") and placed the incident in the previous week.
According to that version, the riders were hunting a man who had recently committed a murder in the neighborhood.
No copy gives the race of Verdun, of the mob, or of the man it sought.
While Verdun was driving his horse and carriage, a band of mounted men came toward him at speed, and he took them for highwaymen.
The pursuers, described as a "mob" and "the lynchers," took him for the murderer they wished to hang.
Verdun whipped his horse and stopped now and then to fire "a wild shot back to the chasers," while they put bullets through the top of his carriage.
The German account says instead that he fired his revolver to show that he was armed.
The riders finally overtook him, and the "mutual blunder was forgiven with drinks all around."
In the German version, the misunderstanding was cleared up and the party recovered from the chase at the nearest inn.
No report of arrests, an inquest or any official response appears in the coverage, and nothing more is said of the murderer the mob had been hunting.
The earliest copy found ran on the front page of the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on 13 August 1881 under the head "Kentucky Manners of the Road."

The same unsigned paragraph then moved through columns of miscellany: "News Chips" in the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic on 18 August, and "In a Nutshell" in the River Falls Journal and the Iowa County Democrat of Mineral Point, Wisconsin, on 25 and 26 August.
It also appeared among briefs in the Pioche Weekly Record of Nevada on 27 August and the Idaho Semi-Weekly World on 30 August.
The copies differ by a letter: some say "a desperate fight and pursuit," others "a desperate flight and pursuit."
The Washingtoner Journal, a German-language paper, retold the story at greater length under the head "Beinahe das Opfer eines Mißverständnisses" (nearly the victim of a misunderstanding).
Every version treated the mob's readiness to hang a suspect, and its gunfire, as material for humor rather than as a crime, and none named a source.

accounts.label: Unattributed news paragraph
accounts.gist: A Kentucky mob took Verdun for a murderer and he took them for highwaymen; after a chase with shots both ways he was overtaken and the 'mutual blunder' was forgiven with drinks.

accounts.label: German-language version
accounts.gist: A band of riders took the salesman Verdun for a man who had recently committed a murder nearby and chased him to hang him; he fired a revolver to show he was armed, they riddled his wagon, and once overtaken the misunderstanding was cleared up at the nearest inn.

framing.detail: The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran it as a comic item under the head 'Kentucky Manners of the Road', ending with the blunder 'forgiven with drinks all around'.
The Washingtoner Journal headed it 'Beinahe das Opfer eines Mißverständnisses' (nearly the victim of a misunderstanding) among light miscellany.
Weeklies in North Carolina, Wisconsin, Nevada and Idaho reprinted the paragraph unchanged in columns of briefs such as 'News Chips' and 'In a Nutshell'.

conflicts.note: A one-letter variant between copies of the same paragraph; 'flight' fits the chase described, and no hand-to-hand fight is reported in any copy.

record_check.dossier: Not stated in any copy; nothing in the coverage marks Verdun or the mob as Black or white.
A mob intent on hanging a supposed murderer chased and fired on Verdun, but released him when the mistake was found; no one was hurt.
Before 13 August 1881; the German version of 20 August says 'last week'. No exact date is given.
No town or county is named; only 'Kentucky'.
